chunks: Too many vias in a power plane. The question: What happens if you have too many vias through a power plane?
A power plane is a sheet of copper that carries current to chips. Every via that passes through it without connecting still cuts a clearance hole in it.
If the holes get close together, the copper between them becomes narrow necks.
Current must squeeze through, which adds resistance, voltage drop and heat, and also raises inductance (opposition to fast current changes).
You avoid it by staggering vias and shrinking the holes.
Picture a wide road with a row of concrete pillars across it. If the pillars are far apart, traffic flows around them with little trouble.
If they are packed close together, all the cars must squeeze through the narrow gaps, and traffic backs up.
The current in a plane is the traffic, and the gaps between holes are the narrow lanes.
A row of antipads (white circles) forces current (grey flow lines) to squeeze through the narrow webs between them (red marks the web width W ).
Along the row the copper cross-section drops to (p-d a) over p , so the current density there rises by p over (p-d a) .
Power plane: a solid copper layer that delivers a supply voltage across the board. Antipad: the clearance hole in a plane around a via that does not connect to it.
Neck: the narrow strip of copper left between two nearby holes. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square of copper of any size.
For standard 1 oz (35 µm thick) copper it is about 0. 49 milliohms. IR drop: the voltage lost as current flows through resistance, V equals I times R .
A neck that is 10 mm long and 0. 1 mm wide is 100 squares long. Its resistance is 100 times 0. 49 milliohms = 49 milliohms. Carrying 3 amps, it drops 3 times 0. 049 = 0.
147 volts, which is 147 millivolts. That is a big loss on a 1 volts supply. A neck 1 mm wide is only 10 squares, 4. 9 milliohms, or 15 millivolts.
This is a worst case with all the current in one channel; real via fields have many channels in parallel. That is the whole idea: narrower copper means more resistance and heat.
"Each via that doesn't connect to a power plane still cuts an antipad hole.

Too many and the copper between holes becomes narrow necks, so resistance, IR drop and current density rise, causing hot spots; the plane inductance rises and signals referencing it lose their return path.
I stagger vias, shrink antipads, keep wide copper bridges, and use heavier copper or more planes."
